Microsoft Just Offered 60,000 Buyouts. Are Layoffs Really Rising?

2026-11-05

Subscribe for one money story a week

About this video

Microsoft just offered buyouts to about 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its workforce. So are layoffs really surging? The government's own data tells a very different story. Penny the coin breaks down the job market with official data: what a buyout is (and why so few people take one), whether layoffs are really rising, weekly jobless claims, how we got here, the real problem (hiring has slowed way down), the great stay, tech jobs and AI, which industry is still hiring, two numbers to watch for a recession, and what it all means for you. 0:00 Intro: 60,000 buyouts 0:30 Buyout vs layoff 1:27 Are layoffs really rising? 2:05 The weekly warning sign 2:35 How we got here 3:05 The real problem: hiring 3:51 The great stay 4:13 Tech jobs and AI 4:54 Who is still hiring? 5:31 Two numbers to watch 6:02 What this means for you 6:46 Recap Data: Layoffs and discharges, quits, job openings and hires rate (BLS JOLTS: JTSLDL, JTSQUL, JTSJOL, JTSHIR); initial jobless claims (US Dept. of Labor: ICSA); payrolls by industry (BLS: PAYEMS, CES6562000001, MANEMP, USINFO); unemployment (BLS: UNRATE, UNEMPLOY, UEMPMEAN); Sahm rule recession indicator (SAHMREALTIME); Fed funds target (DFEDTARU); retrieved from FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, through October 2026. This week, Microsoft offered buyouts to about 60,000 employees. That's roughly a quarter of its entire workforce. Headlines are full of layoffs and artificial intelligence. So, is your job in danger? Let's skip the panic and look at the government's own numbers, because they tell a very different story than the headlines. And stick around, because one industry is still hiring like crazy, and it's probably not the one you'd guess. First, a buyout is not a layoff. In a layoff, the company decides you're leaving. A buyout is an offer. The company pays you to leave voluntarily, usually with severance based on how long you've worked there. Long-time employees usually get the biggest checks. Microsoft's offer goes to staff at the vice president level and below in the US, Canada, India, and the UK, and they have until early December to decide. It's actually Microsoft's second buyout this year. According to reports, an earlier offer went to employees near retirement age, and more than 30% of the roughly 8,750 people who were eligible took it. Microsoft is spending heavily on artificial intelligence infrastructure, and says it wants to control headcount while avoiding layoffs. And here's a surprising detail. At other big tech companies with similar programs, only about 3 to 5% of people said yes. The downside for companies is that the people most likely to take the money are often the ones who can easily find another job. So, are layoffs really surging across America? This is the official count, from a monthly survey of about 21,000 employers run by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. In August, US employers laid off or discharged about 1.64 million workers. That sounds like a lot, until you compare it. In 2019, before the pandemic, the average was about 1.82 million a month. As a share of all jobs, it's about 1% a month now, compared with 1.2% in 2019. And remember March 2020? Almost 13 million people were laid off in a single month. Today is nowhere near that. Economists also watch a faster signal: new claims for unemployment benefits, reported every single week. Last week, about 194,000 people filed a new claim. In 2019, the weekly average was about 218,000. If mass layoffs were spreading across the country, this number would be shooting up. So far, it isn't. The unemployment rate says the same thing. It's 4.2%, a little higher than the 3.7% average of 2019, but still low by historical standards. To understand today, rewind to 2021 and 2022. After the pandemic, companies couldn't hire fast enough. Job openings hit record highs, and a record number of people quit for better pay. Some called it the great resignation. Then the Federal Reserve raised interest rates 11 times to fight inflation. Borrowing got expensive, companies slowed down, and hiring cooled off. That's exactly what higher rates are designed to do, and it's a big reason the job market feels so different today. So if layoffs are low, why does the job market feel so scary? Because the big change isn't firing. It's hiring. In March 2022, there were about 12.3 million open jobs in America. Now there are about 7.1 million. Back then, there were 2 open jobs for every unemployed person. Now there's about 1. And companies are hiring slowly. In August, only 3.3% of workers were new hires, compared with 3.9% in 2019. Economists call this a low-hire, low-fire job market. If you have a job, it's fairly safe. But if you lose one, finding the next one takes longer. The average unemployed person has now been looking for about 25 weeks, compared with about 22 weeks in 2019. You can see the nervousness in another number: how many people quit. In April 2022, a record 4.5 million Americans quit their jobs in a single month. Now it's about 3.1 million. People aren't leaving, because they're not sure they'll find something better. Some people call it the great stay. Fewer people quitting also means fewer openings for everyone else. Now, the tech industry. The government's information sector, which includes software publishers, telecom, and media, shows the pressure clearly. It peaked at about 3.12 million jobs in November 2022. Today it's about 2.74 million. That's about 376,000 fewer jobs, or roughly 12%. Many tech companies say they hired too fast during the pandemic, and now they're shifting money toward artificial intelligence, like the giant data centers Microsoft is building. So is AI replacing these workers? Microsoft says it is not replacing them with AI agents. But the pressure to cut costs while spending billions on AI is very real. So who is still hiring? First, the big picture. Over the past 12 months, the US economy added about 496,000 jobs in total. That's about 41,000 a month. In 2019, it was about 165,000 a month. Now the surprise. Health care alone added about 520,000 jobs. That's more than the entire economy added overall, which means many other industries actually shrank. The information sector lost about 120,000 jobs over the same period, while manufacturing barely moved. Hospitals, clinics, and home health care are where the hiring is. So how will you know if things are really getting worse? Watch two numbers. The first is weekly jobless claims. It's about 194 thousand now. Many economists treat a steady climb toward 300 thousand as a warning sign. The second is the Sahm rule, a recession signal created by economist Claudia Sahm. It compares the recent unemployment rate with its low over the past year. Right now, it reads 0.00. When it reaches 0.5, a recession has usually already started. Today, it's nowhere close. So what does this mean for you? Here's what the data suggests. One: in a low-hire market, an emergency fund matters more, because a job search can take longer. Many experts suggest three to six months of expenses. Two: if you're thinking about quitting, line up the next job first. Three: keep your skills current. Learning to use AI tools in your own field can make you more valuable, not less. And four: if you're ever offered a buyout, compare the severance with how long a job search might take in your field, and talk to a professional before you decide. And five: if you're ever laid off, file for unemployment benefits right away. Rules differ by state, and taking a voluntary buyout can affect whether you qualify, so check with your state first. So, layoffs are not surging. The real story is a job market where hiring has slowed way down, and tech is feeling it the most.
